user_question: What documentation is required to open a bank account in Toronto?
final_response:
# Documents Required to Open a Bank Account in Toronto

Federally regulated banks follow federal account-opening rules across Canada. Credit unions can follow different provincial requirements, so exact requirements should be checked with the institution you choose.

---

## Your Legal Right to Open an Account

FCAC provides the federal rules for access to a basic personal bank account at federally regulated banks, including identification requirements and limited exceptions. Check the current FCAC guidance and the chosen bank's own requirements before applying.

---

## Core ID Requirement: Two Routes

FCAC sets out two ways to meet the requirement, and you must provide **original** identification, not photocopies. [source](https://www.ansariimmigration.com/post/how-to-open-a-bank-account-in-canada-as-a-newcomer-a-complete-2026-guide)

### Route 1 — Two Documents (Standard)
One identification route uses acceptable original documents that together establish the required identity information. Check FCAC's current official list for the permitted document combinations.

**Common documents that count:**
- A passport, Permanent Resident (PR) card, or Canadian driver's licence all work as primary photo ID. [source](https://www.wealthsimple.com/en-ca/learn/how-to-open-a-bank-account-in-canada-documents-needed)
- Secondary ID options include: a PR card, study permit, work permit, Canadian government employee ID, a credit card with name and signature, or a document from another financial institution confirming an existing account. [source](https://www.moneymapcanada.com/blog/newcomer-bank-account-canada)
- A passport is the most universally accepted document across all Canadian financial institutions. Some banks also accept a driver's licence from your home country when presented alongside your passport. [source](https://www.wealthsimple.com/en-ca/learn/how-to-open-a-bank-account-in-canada-newcomers)

### Route 2 — One Document + Community Vouching
FCAC also provides an alternative identification method in some cases. Check the current official FCAC guidance before relying on that route.

---

## If You Are a Newcomer / Recent Arrival

Newcomers need their immigration document — such as a work permit, PR card, or study permit. [source](https://wealthnorth.ca/banking/chequing/how-to-open-bank-account-canada/) International students are eligible for Canadian bank accounts with their passport, study permit, and proof of enrollment. [source](https://wealthnorth.ca/banking/chequing/how-to-open-bank-account-canada/)

If you plan to rely on an immigration document such as a work or study permit, confirm that document directly with the bank before your appointment.

---

## What You Do NOT Need

You do not need a credit history, a minimum deposit, or a Canadian job offer. [source](https://canadianow.com/how-to-open-bank-account-canada-newcomer/)

**SIN (Social Insurance Number):** You need a SIN eventually for employment, taxes, and registered accounts (TFSA, RRSP, FHSA), but most banks will open a basic chequing or savings account without it. You can add your SIN to the account once you have one. [source](https://www.moneymapcanada.com/blog/newcomer-bank-account-canada)

---

## Online-Only Banks: One Caveat

FCAC notes that institutions operating only online may require you to already have an account at another financial institution before they will open one for you. For a first Canadian account, a bank or credit union with branches is often the smoother route. [source](https://www.ansariimmigration.com/post/how-to-open-a-bank-account-in-canada-as-a-newcomer-a-complete-2026-guide)

---

## If a Bank Refuses You

If you are refused without a legitimate reason, you can ask the bank for a written explanation (they're legally required to provide one). From there, you can contact their internal complaints department, file a complaint with the FCAC, or contact the Ombudsman for Banking Services and Investments (OBSI). [source](https://www.wealthsimple.com/en-ca/learn/how-to-open-a-bank-account-in-canada-documents-needed)

---

## What to Confirm Before You Decide

| Item | Where to Verify |
|---|---|
| Exact document list accepted at a specific bank | Call or visit the bank's Toronto branch directly before your appointment |
| Whether your immigration document (work/study permit) is accepted as standalone ID | Confirm with the specific branch — acceptance can vary |
| SIN application (if not yet obtained) | [Service Canada](https://www.canada.ca/en/employment-social-development/services/sin.html) |
| FCAC's official ID rules | [canada.ca/fcac](https://www.canada.ca/en/financial-consumer-agency.html) |

---

## Confidence

- **Overall confidence:** Medium
- **Overall confidence reason:** The general framework is consistent with federal account-opening guidance, but exact acceptable-document combinations should be confirmed on FCAC's official site and with the chosen institution.
- **Section confidence:**
  - *Legal Right to Open an Account*: High — directly sourced from FCAC-attributed guidance
  - *Two Routes for ID*: High — aligns with FCAC's published framework across multiple consistent sources
  - *Newcomer Documents*: High — consistent across multiple 2026 sources; individual bank acceptance of specific permits should be confirmed directly
  - *What You Do NOT Need*: High — consistent across multiple sources referencing FCAC rules
  - *Online-Only Banks*: High — FCAC-attributed guidance cited by multiple sources
  - *If a Bank Refuses You*: High — statutory right described consistently across sources

# Minimum Balance Requirements for Savings Accounts in Toronto

The short answer: **there is no Toronto-wide minimum balance for savings accounts.** Opening minimums, maintenance minimums, membership deposits, and fee conditions are product-specific and must be checked with the institution.

---

## 3. Credit Unions in Toronto — Membership Share Deposit

Credit unions may have membership-share or minimum-deposit requirements that vary by institution. Confirm the exact current amount and whether it is refundable on the credit union's own account or membership page.

---

## 5. Premium or High-Yield Savings Tiers

Some savings products, especially high-yield tiers at larger banks, may require a minimum balance to **earn a bonus interest rate** (not to keep the account open). Most HISAs don't charge a monthly fee, but some may charge for withdrawals or transfers. Many accounts include a set number of free transactions each month or waive fees if you hold a minimum account balance. [source](https://www.nerdwallet.com/ca/p/best/banking/best-high-interest-savings-accounts) Always read the rate conditions carefully to distinguish the base rate from the promotional or tiered rate.

---

## What to Confirm Before You Decide

|---|---|
| Specific savings account minimum balance terms | The bank's or credit union's own current product page |
| Whether a credit union requires a membership share deposit and how much | Contact the credit union directly |
| Eligibility for a free (no-cost) account as a newcomer | Ask the bank in-branch; compare at FCAC's account comparison tool at fcac-acfc.gc.ca |
| Whether a minimum balance is tied to the account or only to waiving a fee | Read the account's fee schedule from the institution |

user_question: What's the difference between a chequing account and a savings account?
final_response:
## Chequing vs. Savings Accounts in Canada

These two account types serve completely different purposes — understanding both helps you avoid unnecessary fees and make your money work harder.

---

### 🏦 Chequing Account — For Everyday Spending

A chequing account is a deposit account offered by financial institutions for managing day-to-day financial transactions, such as paying bills, making purchases with a debit card, depositing your paycheque, and sending or receiving email money transfers. [source](https://learninghub.prospercanada.org/knowledge/choosing-the-right-chequing-account-and-banking-package/)

Key features:
- You can use it for deposits (cash and cheques), ATM withdrawals, one-time purchases, pre-authorized payments, transfers, and Interac e-Transfer transactions. [source](https://www.td.com/ca/en/personal-banking/advice/day-to-day-banking/chequing-vs-savings-account)
- Some chequing accounts pay interest on deposits, but when they do, the rate is usually lower than a savings account. [source](https://learninghub.prospercanada.org/knowledge/choosing-the-right-chequing-account-and-banking-package/)
- Monthly maintenance fees can range from $4 to over $17 at traditional banks, unless you maintain a minimum balance to have them waived. [source](https://www.neofinancial.com/blog/difference-between-chequing-and-savings-accounts-in-canada) No-fee chequing options are also widely available.

---

### 💰 Savings Account — For Growing Money You Don't Need Daily

A savings account is designed to help you save money, letting you earn interest on the money you deposit so your balance grows over time. [source](https://www.finder.com/ca/banking/types-of-bank-accounts)

Key features:
- You earn interest on savings account deposits that provide a return on your funds. While rates can be modest, you earn extra money without doing anything beyond making deposits. [source](https://www.innovationcu.ca/personal/advice-tools/blog/2023/chequing-account-vs-savings-account.html)
- Direct debit purchases or bill payments from a savings account typically trigger steep per-transaction fees [source](https://www.neofinancial.com/blog/difference-between-chequing-and-savings-accounts-in-canada) — savings accounts are not built for daily spending.
- A savings account is a good place to build an emergency fund covering three to six months of essential expenses. The money stays liquid enough to transfer into your chequing account within a business day if needed, but sits apart from daily spending. [source](https://www.neofinancial.com/blog/difference-between-chequing-and-savings-accounts-in-canada)

---

### ⚖️ Key Differences at a Glance

| Feature | Chequing | Savings |
|---|---|---|
| **Primary use** | Daily spending & bills | Storing & growing money |
| **Interest earned** | Little to none | Higher rate |
| **Transactions** | Unlimited or high limit | Often limited; fees may apply for excess transactions |
| **Monthly fees** | Common (but no-fee options exist) | Often lower or none |
| **Debit card access** | Yes | Usually not directly |

---

### 🔒 Deposit Insurance

Both chequing and savings accounts are generally insured by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation (CDIC) for banks, federally regulated credit unions, and loan and trust companies, up to $100,000 per depositor for each ownership category. [source](https://www.forbes.com/advisor/ca/banking/chequing-vs-savings-accounts/) Provincially regulated credit unions and caisses populaires are covered by provincial deposit insurance plans, such as the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA) for Ontario credit unions. [source](https://www.forbes.com/advisor/ca/banking/chequing-vs-savings-accounts/)

---

### 💡 Do You Need Both?

Chequing accounts handle your daily spending and recurring bills, while savings accounts help you build savings, protect against unexpected expenses, and meet goals — and you don't have to choose just one. It's often beneficial to have both a chequing and a savings account. [source](https://www.forbes.com/advisor/ca/banking/chequing-vs-savings-accounts/)

One account trying to do both jobs usually means you're either paying fees you shouldn't, or missing out on interest you should be earning. [source](https://landedmoney.ca/chequing-vs-savings-accounts-canada/)

You can also explore **Tax-Free Savings Accounts (TFSAs)**, which allow interest earned to grow tax-free — a popular option in Canada for medium- and long-term savings goals. The FCAC's [Account Comparison Tool](https://itools-ioutils.fcac-acfc.gc.ca/ACT-OCC/SearchFilter-eng.aspx) lets you compare specific chequing and savings accounts side-by-side by province.

---

## What to Confirm Before You Decide

- **Monthly fees and minimum balances**: These vary significantly by institution and account tier — check directly with your bank or credit union.
- **Transaction limits on savings accounts**: Some institutions cap free monthly withdrawals; confirm the specific limit for any account you consider.
- **No-fee/low-fee options**: If you're price-sensitive, the FCAC's commitment on low-cost and no-cost accounts (effective December 2025) may be relevant — verify with your bank what qualifying products they offer.

Nothing else material remains unresolved for this general question.

---

## Confidence
- **Overall confidence:** High
- **Overall confidence reason:** The core distinctions between chequing and savings accounts in Canada are well-supported by multiple consistent sources, including FCAC-affiliated guidance and major Canadian financial institutions.
- **Section confidence:**
  - Chequing Account: High — directly supported by FCAC-aligned and bank first-party sources
  - Savings Account: High — consistent across multiple sources
  - Key Differences Table: High — derived directly from the evidence above
  - Deposit Insurance: Medium — supported by a secondary (Forbes Canada) source rather than a direct CDIC or FSRA page; the $100,000 figure and category structure are consistent with known CDIC rules but the exact current CDIC categories were not retrieved from CDIC directly this session
  - Do You Need Both: High — consistent across multiple sources

## RBC's Community Sponsorships and Charitable Giving in Toronto and Canada

Yes — RBC actively provides both financial donations and sponsorships to local Toronto and broader Canadian community programs and registered charities, primarily through the **RBC Foundation**.

---

### The RBC Foundation: How It Works

RBC Foundation is a Canadian Registered Charity and Private Foundation. It is solely funded by RBC and its subsidiaries, providing donations exclusively from RBC and its subsidiaries' annual earnings — not from third-party or client donations. [source](https://www.newswire.ca/news-releases/rbc-foundation-announces-recipients-of-the-2026-community-spaces-grant-to-advance-environmental-sustainability-and-accessibility-in-buildings-and-spaces-808178520.html)

The RBC Foundation Recognition Guidelines set out the expectations and procedures for recognizing gifts made to other Canadian registered charities or qualified donees under the *Income Tax Act*. [source](https://www.rbc.com/our-impact/apply-for-funding/community-investments-canada.html)

RBC, together with the RBC Foundation in Canada and the U.S., has committed to making $2 billion in community investments by 2035. [source](https://www.rbc.com/our-impact/)

---

### Key Programs That Fund Toronto and Ontario Charities

**1. RBC Foundation Community Spaces Grant**

Toronto is one of 35 Canadian towns and cities impacted by a donation from the 2025 RBC Foundation Community Spaces Grant (formerly the RBC Foundation Community Infrastructure Fund). [source](https://www.renewcanada.net/sponsored-how-rbc-foundation-community-spaces-grant-is-supporting-important-infrastructure-across-the-country/)

The grant is open to hospitals, cultural institutions, community centres, and other registered charities in Canada. [source](https://www.renewcanada.net/sponsored-how-rbc-foundation-community-spaces-grant-is-supporting-important-infrastructure-across-the-country/) The RBC Foundation Community Spaces Grant provided nearly C$10 million in 2025 to fund the retrofits, repairs, or upgrades of existing community spaces and the construction of new spaces. [source](https://www.rbc.com/our-impact/)

**2. WoodGreen Foundation – Toronto-Specific Commitment**

RBC Foundation announced a $1 million commitment over five years to WoodGreen Foundation in support of its Financial Empowerment – Homelessness Prevention Program in Toronto, providing counselling, tax filing, and financial literacy workshops to homeless and precariously housed individuals. [source](https://www.rbc.com/our-impact/)

**3. RBC Stronger Nonprofits Program (Launched 2026)**

In May 2026, RBC and RBC Foundation unveiled the RBC Stronger Nonprofits Program and website as part of their ongoing commitment to help strengthen the capacity and resilience of the nonprofit sector. The new online hub connects Canadian charitable organizations with essential capacity-building resources, programs, and supports. [source](https://www.newswire.ca/news-releases/rbc-unveils-new-program-and-online-hub-designed-to-help-strengthen-canada-s-nonprofit-sector-amid-unprecedented-strain-837153162.html)

**4. RBC Charity Day (Capital Markets)**

In 2025, RBC donated $7 million to over 70 youth-focused organizations. Since its inception in 2015, RBC Charity Day has invested $55 million in 150+ charities to support youth around the world. [source](https://www.rbccm.com/en/insights/charityday)

**5. Employee-Driven Giving**

RBC offers employees opportunities to support communities in ways that align with their individual interests, together raising over C$30 million in donations to charities and volunteering 340,000 hours globally. [source](https://www.rbc.com/our-impact/)

---

### Sponsorships (Separate From Donations)

RBC accepts sponsorship proposals through its community-investment process. Current eligibility, intake details, and terms should be confirmed on RBC's own funding pages. [source](https://www.rbc.com/community-social-impact/)

---

### How a Toronto Charity Can Apply

Applications for donations and sponsorships are accepted year-round. [source](https://www.rbc.com/community-social-impact/)

RBC will consider funding up to 50% of a specific project or program budget for donation requests. [source](https://www.rbc.com/community-social-impact/apply-for-funding/funding-guidelines-eligibility.html)

RBC receives far more applications than it can fund in any given year. While every application is reviewed, alignment with its priorities does not guarantee funding. [source](https://www.rbc.com/our-impact/apply-for-funding/index.html)

The application portal is at **rbc.com/apply-for-funding** (community-investments-canada page).

---

Yes — TD Canada Trust offers a comprehensive suite of foreign currency exchange services in Canada.

The main service types are:

- **Foreign currency accounts** — TD allows you to hold funds in a foreign currency account or a U.S. dollar account. [source](https://www.knightsbridgefx.com/td-foreign-exchange-centre-rates-fees-and-better-alternatives-for-canadians/)
- **Foreign currency bank drafts** — Bank drafts are available in several foreign currencies and are guaranteed funds, serving as an alternative to cash or cheque when sending foreign currency. [source](https://www.td.com/ca/en/business-banking/solutions/small-business/currency-exchange-services)

TD Foreign Exchange Centre locations in Ontario include:

- **Toronto** — 2263 Yonge Street (Branch #990)
- **Mississauga** — Square One Shopping Centre, 100 City Centre Drive (Branch #0093)

- **Currency availability at your specific branch:** Not all currencies are stocked at every location. Confirm with your branch or call TD at 1-866-222-3456.
- **Ordering cash in advance:** You can call TD to order foreign currency cash for pick-up within 3–7 business days at your preferred branch. [source](https://www.td.com/ca/en/personal-banking/solutions/currency-exchange-services)

user_question: What is the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation (CDIC)?
final_response:
## What Is the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation (CDIC)?

### Overview

The Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation (CDIC) has been protecting people's insured deposits for more than 55 years. The Corporation provides deposit insurance, resolves its member financial institutions in the event they fail, and promotes and contributes to the stability of Canada's financial system. [source](https://www.cdic.ca/about/corporate-reporting-disclosure/summary-of-the-corporate-plan/)

Founded in 1967, CDIC is backed by the federal government and funded by premiums its members pay, not by taxpayers. [source](https://www.lodavo.ca/blog/cdic-deposit-insurance-canada) CDIC was established by the Government of Canada to protect deposits in case of bank failure. Coverage is **free and automatic** when you bank with a member institution. [source](https://www.cdic.ca/)

---

### Who Are CDIC Members?

CDIC's 84 members include banks, federally regulated credit unions, and trust and loan companies. [source](https://www.cdic.ca/about/corporate-reporting-disclosure/summary-of-the-corporate-plan/) Each CDIC member institution must pay annual premiums on insured deposits as a condition of membership. These premiums constitute a reserve fund which CDIC would draw from in order to resolve the failure of any of its members. [source](https://www.cdic.ca/financial-professionals/member-institutions/premiums/)

> **Important:** Most provincially regulated credit unions are covered by provincial deposit insurance rather than CDIC. Federally regulated credit unions can be CDIC members, so verify the institution's status directly with CDIC.

You can verify whether a specific institution is a CDIC member at [cdic.ca](https://www.cdic.ca).

---

### How Much Coverage Do You Get?

CDIC provides deposit insurance of up to **$100,000** for each of the **nine insured account categories** at each CDIC member institution. [source](https://www.canada.ca/en/department-finance/news/2026/09/government-of-canada-announces-appointments-to-the-canada-deposit-insurance-corporation.html) Depositors holding deposits in more than one category can have more than $100,000 in total coverage. [source](https://www.cdic.ca/depositors/whats-covered/)

The nine separately insured categories, as listed by CDIC, are:


1. Deposits held **in one name**
2. Deposits held **in trust**
3. **Joint** deposits
4. Deposits in **RRSPs**
5. Deposits in **RRIFs**
6. Deposits in **TFSAs**
7. Deposits in **RESPs**
8. Deposits in **RDSPs**
9. Deposits in a **First Home Savings Account (FHSA)**
 [source](https://www.cdic.ca/about/corporate-reporting-disclosure/infosource/)

---

### What Is (and Isn't) Covered?

CDIC protects eligible deposits in Canadian and foreign currency for up to $100,000 (Canadian dollars) in each of CDIC's insurance categories. This protection applies to deposits held in registered accounts such as RRSPs and TFSAs and non-registered accounts such as savings, chequing, and joint accounts. [source](https://www.cdic.ca/wp-content/uploads/cdic-protecting-your-deposits-brochure-en.pdf)

CDIC protects eligible deposits up to $100,000 (principal and interest combined) per insured category, per member institution — but this limit **does not apply** to mutual funds, stocks, bonds, ETFs, or cryptocurrency. [source](https://insurevest.ca/en/articles/ca/cdic-deposit-insurance-2026-what-credit-union-mergers-mean-for-your-savings)

CDIC covers one specific thing: the failure of a member institution. It doesn't reimburse fraud, a scam, a hacked account, or an investment that drops in value. [source](https://www.lodavo.ca/blog/cdic-deposit-insurance-canada)

---

### What Happens If a Member Bank Fails?

CDIC is a federal Crown corporation that insures more than $1 trillion in deposits held in member institutions. In the rare event a member institution faces failure, it steps in to ensure you have access to your insured deposits, using tools such as supporting the sale of a troubled financial institution to a healthy one, or, if necessary, reimbursing depositors directly. [source](https://www.cdic.ca/depositors/whats-covered/)

# TD Bank Canada — Loan & Credit Card Product Overview

Here is a structured overview of TD Canada Trust's personal loan and credit card products, drawn from TD's own pages (current as of September 2026).

---

## Credit Cards

TD offers a range of credit cards, from student and business cards to low-interest and rewards cards. [source](https://www.nerdwallet.com/ca/p/best/credit-cards/best-td-bank-credit-cards-canada) Getting the right TD credit card starts with comparing and finding one compatible with your income, spending habits, and financial goals. [source](https://www.td.com/ca/en/personal-banking/products/credit-cards/browse-all)

### 1. Travel Rewards — Aeroplan Cards
TD has a suite of co-branded Aeroplan (Air Canada) credit cards:
- **TD® Aeroplan® Visa Infinite\* Card** — annual fee of $139 (first-year rebate available), with a purchase interest rate of 21.99%/22.99% and earn rates of 1x–1.5x Aeroplan points. [source](https://www.nerdwallet.com/ca/p/best/credit-cards/best-td-bank-credit-cards-canada)
- **TD® Aeroplan® Visa Platinum\* Card** — annual fee of $89 (first-year rebate available), 21.99%/22.99% interest rate, and earn rates of 0.67x–1x points. [source](https://www.nerdwallet.com/ca/p/best/credit-cards/best-td-bank-credit-cards-canada)
- **TD® Aeroplan® Visa Infinite Privilege\* Card** — the top-tier Aeroplan card with premium travel perks.

### 2. Travel Rewards — TD Rewards Cards
- **TD First Class Travel® Visa Infinite\* Card** — earns outsized TD Rewards Points when booking through Expedia for TD, and includes a $100 annual travel credit and lounge access. [source](https://www.nerdwallet.com/ca/p/best/credit-cards/best-td-bank-credit-cards-canada)
- **TD Platinum Travel® Visa\* Card** — a mid-tier TD Rewards travel card.

### 3. Cash Back Cards
TD Cash Back credit cards offer a higher earn rate on categories such as Grocery, Gas & Electric Vehicle Charging, Public Transit, Recurring Bill Payments, and Streaming, Digital Gaming & Media Purchases. [source](https://www.td.com/ca/en/personal-banking/products/credit-cards/cash-back) You can earn 1% or 3% depending on the card you choose; not all TD cash back cards offer the same features and benefits, so it's important to evaluate the annual fee, earn rate, and other benefits. [source](https://www.td.com/ca/en/personal-banking/products/credit-cards/cash-back)

Key cards:
- **TD Cash Back Visa Infinite\* Card** — higher earn rate, annual fee
- **TD Cash Back Visa\* Card** — no-annual-fee entry-level cash back option

### 4. No Annual Fee Cards
- **TD Rewards Visa\* Card** — no annual fee, earns 1x–4x TD Rewards Points depending on category, and has a standard purchase interest rate of 21.99%/22.99%. [source](https://www.nerdwallet.com/ca/p/best/credit-cards/best-td-bank-credit-cards-canada)

### 5. Low-Interest Card
- **TD Low Rate Visa\* Card** — designed for financial flexibility on everyday purchases, with a low annual interest rate of 12.90% for residents outside Quebec (13.90% in Quebec) on purchases and cash advances. [source](https://milesopedia.com/en/cards/td/)

### 6. U.S. Dollar Card
TD also offers a U.S. Dollar credit card [source](https://www.td.com/ca/en/personal-banking/products/auto-finance), useful for those who make frequent cross-border purchases.

### 7. Student & Newcomer Cards
For those new to Canada, some cards offer accessible options with no fees and no personal minimum income requirement, available through the TD New to Canada Banking Package. [source](https://springfinancial.ca/blog/lifestyle/best-td-credit-cards-canada/) Student cards are also available, ranging from no annual fees to cash back and travel rewards, to help students start building their credit history. [source](https://www.td.com/ca/en/personal-banking/solutions/student-banking/student-credit-cards)

---

## Loans & Lines of Credit

### 1. Personal Loan
TD Bank offers personal loans of up to $50,000 with loan terms from 1 to 7 years. Funds can be used to cover expenses such as home renovations or debt consolidation, with fixed or variable rate options. [source](https://loanscanada.ca/lender/td-bank/) Personal loan payments can be made monthly, weekly, bi-weekly, or semi-monthly. [source](https://www.td.com/ca/en/personal-banking/advice/borrowing/loan-vs-line-of-credit)

### 2. Personal Line of Credit (PLOC)
For more flexible financing, TD's Personal Line of Credit provides access to extra money on an ongoing, as-needed basis — from $5,000 to $50,000 — and you can pay back as much or as little as you want, as long as you stay within the credit limit. Interest is only charged on the amount withdrawn. [source](https://loanscanada.ca/lender/td-bank/)

### 3. Home Equity FlexLine (HELOC)
The TD Home Equity FlexLine combines the flexibility of a line of credit with the stability of a mortgage loan, letting you use your home equity to secure credit for things like home improvements, education costs, or other important goals. [source](https://td.com/ca/en/personal-banking/products/borrowing/lines-of-credit/td-home-equity-flexline) It has two components: a revolving portion (a line of credit) and a term portion. [source](https://td.com/ca/en/personal-banking/products/borrowing/lines-of-credit/td-home-equity-flexline)

### 4. Auto Loan / Car Loan
For purchasing a vehicle (up to 5 years old), TD auto loans are secured against the vehicle, allow you to pay it off with fixed regular payments, and may offer a lower rate than an unsecured loan. [source](https://www.td.com/ca/en/personal-banking/advice/borrowing/types-of-loans-and-lines-of-credit)

### 5. Student Line of Credit
This line of credit features a low interest rate specific for students and has flexible access to credit, with credit limits specific to the program (undergraduate, college, graduate, or professional). Interest-only monthly payments are required while in school and for 24 months after leaving. [source](https://www.td.com/ca/en/personal-banking/advice/borrowing/types-of-loans-and-lines-of-credit) TD also offers a **Professional Student Line of Credit** for graduate/professional programs.

### 6. RSP Loan
An RSP Loan allows you to borrow up to your unused RSP contribution room for the current year, is amortized over 1 year, and offers the option to defer payments (up to 120 days in most provinces). Any tax refund received can be used to repay all or part of the loan. [source](https://www.td.com/ca/en/personal-banking/advice/borrowing/types-of-loans-and-lines-of-credit)

### 7. Mortgages
TD offers various mortgage products, including fixed-rate and variable-rate options, for buying a first home, a second property, or tapping into home equity through the TD Home Equity FlexLine. [source](https://loanscanada.ca/lender/td-bank/)

user_question: What information do I need to set up direct deposit properly?
final_response:
# Setting Up Direct Deposit in Canada: What You Need

Direct deposit in Canada is straightforward — every payer (employer, CRA, Service Canada) requires the same three pieces of banking information, plus sometimes a way to verify them. Here's a complete breakdown.

---

## The Three Core Banking Numbers

The process differs slightly depending on who you are setting direct deposit up with — an employer, CRA, or Service Canada — but the banking information required is identical in all cases. [source](https://wealthnorth.ca/banking/transfers/how-to-set-up-direct-deposit-canada/)

You need:
- **Transit number** — 5 digits identifying your branch
- **Institution number** — 3 digits identifying your bank
- **Account number** — 7–12 digits for your specific account [source](https://bremo.io/direct-deposit-canada)

All three are required; providing only two will result in a rejected setup or a returned deposit. [source](https://wealthnorth.ca/banking/transfers/how-to-set-up-direct-deposit-canada/)

---

## Where to Find These Numbers

These can be found on a void cheque, in your online banking portal, in your bank's mobile app, or on your bank statement. [source](https://bremo.io/direct-deposit-canada)

- **Void cheque:** A void cheque is a personal cheque with "VOID" written across it. It contains your institution number, transit number, and account number printed at the bottom in MICR (magnetic ink character recognition) format. [source](https://wealthnorth.ca/banking/chequing/direct-deposit-canada/)
- **Electronic void cheque:** You can use a void paper cheque or you can get an electronic void cheque using your online banking. [source](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-services-procurement/services/payments-to-from-government/direct-deposit.html) Almost all Canadian banks let you generate a direct deposit information PDF or void cheque image through online banking or their mobile app. [source](https://wealthnorth.ca/banking/chequing/direct-deposit-canada/)

> **Tip:** Double-check all three numbers before submitting — a transposed digit in your account number will cause the deposit to reject. [source](https://wealthnorth.ca/banking/transfers/how-to-set-up-direct-deposit-canada/)

---

## What to Submit to Your Payer

### Employer / Payroll
Ask your employer's HR or payroll department for a direct deposit enrollment form. Most payroll platforms have a standardized form; some allow employees to enter banking information themselves through an employee self-service portal. [source](https://wealthnorth.ca/banking/transfers/how-to-set-up-direct-deposit-canada/)

Most employers and government agencies will accept a direct deposit authorization form with your banking numbers typed in (no void cheque required). [source](https://wealthnorth.ca/banking/chequing/direct-deposit-canada/) However, attaching a void cheque or a bank-generated direct deposit form is also widely accepted.

Allow 1–2 pay cycles after enrollment. Most payroll systems process direct deposit changes before the next payroll run, but some require a full cycle. [source](https://wealthnorth.ca/banking/transfers/how-to-set-up-direct-deposit-canada/)

### CRA (Tax Refunds & Benefits)
You can sign up for or update direct deposit to receive your tax refunds and benefit payments faster and securely, directly in your account at a Canadian bank or credit union. [source](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/about-canada-revenue-agency-cra/direct-deposit.html)

You can enroll via:
- **CRA My Account** (online) — enter your transit number, institution number, and account number directly.
- **Your bank's online/mobile banking** — TD, RBC, Scotiabank, BMO, and CIBC all support CRA sign-in partner [source](https://bremo.io/direct-deposit-canada) integrations that let you register without leaving your bank's app.

For CRA setup you will also need your **date of birth** and **Social Insurance Number (SIN)** to authenticate your identity when logging into My Account.

### Government Benefits (Service Canada — EI, CPP, OAS)
Canada Pension Plan (CPP) and Old Age Security (OAS) are set up separately through Service Canada. [source](https://wealthnorth.ca/banking/chequing/direct-deposit-canada/) The same three banking numbers apply, but the enrollment is done through your **My Service Canada Account** or by submitting a paper form to Service Canada.

> If you are receiving multiple payments, you may need to contact more than one government department to set up direct deposit or change your banking information. [source](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-services-procurement/services/payments-to-from-government/direct-deposit.html)

---

## Quick Reference Summary

| What You Need | Details |
|---|---|
| Transit number | 5 digits (your branch) |
| Institution number | 3 digits (your bank) |
| Account number | 7–12 digits (your account) |
| Proof/verification | Void cheque or bank-generated direct deposit form |
| For CRA/Service Canada | Also your SIN and date of birth (for identity verification) |

---

## What to Confirm Before You Decide

- **Employer portal:** Confirm with your HR or payroll team whether they use a paper form or a self-service portal (e.g., Workday, ADP, Dayforce), as submission steps vary.
- **CRA vs. Service Canada:** Confirm which agency administers each benefit you receive — they maintain separate direct deposit records and you must register with each independently.
- **Your bank's direct deposit form:** If you don't have cheques, log into your bank's app or online portal to download an official pre-authorized debit/direct deposit PDF — this is accepted in place of a void cheque by virtually all Canadian payers.

---

## Confidence
- **Overall confidence:** High
- **Overall confidence reason:** The three core banking numbers and the process steps are consistent across the Canada.ca official source, CRA's own guidance, and multiple corroborating sources.
- **Section confidence:**
  - The Three Core Banking Numbers: High — directly supported by multiple consistent sources including Canada.ca
  - Where to Find These Numbers: High — confirmed by Canada.ca and first-party bank guidance
  - Employer / Payroll Setup: High — well-supported; exact timing may vary by employer system
  - CRA Setup: High — supported by CRA's own pages and CIBC's first-party page for the bank integration method
  - Service Canada Setup: Medium — confirmed that CPP/OAS use Service Canada separately, but specific My Service Canada Account steps were not retrieved from a first-party source in this search

user_question: What steps can I take to build a Canadian credit history from scratch?
final_response:
# Building a Canadian Credit History From Scratch

Foreign credit history does not automatically become part of your Canadian credit file, although some lenders may use separate services to consider international credit history. The steps below move from foundational setup to active credit-building habits and monitoring.

---

## Step 1 — Get Your Social Insurance Number (SIN) and Open a Bank Account

Start by getting a Social Insurance Number (SIN), then open a Canadian bank account. [source](https://www.wealthsimple.com/en-ca/learn/how-to-build-credit) A chequing account won't generate a credit score on its own, but it establishes a relationship with a financial institution and gives you a place to manage bill payments. [source](https://www.neofinancial.com/blog/how-to-build-your-credit-from-scratch-as-a-canadian-immigrant) While a bank account isn't always necessary, once you have an account open it becomes easier to manage your money and additional credit products you may open with the same bank. [source](https://nomoredebts.org/blog/learn-about-credit/credit-cards-for-newcomers-to-canada-where-to-start-building-credit)

---

## Step 2 — Get Your First Credit Product (Two Main Routes)

### Route A: Secured Credit Card
A secured credit card requires a refundable cash deposit, which typically becomes your credit limit. If you deposit $500, your limit is $500. The deposit reduces lender risk, making approval accessible to people with no credit history. Secured cards report to the credit bureaus the same way regular cards do, so responsible use builds your credit history just as effectively. [source](https://www.wealthsimple.com/en-ca/learn/how-to-build-credit)

Over time, as your credit improves, you may qualify to upgrade to an unsecured card and have your deposit returned. [source](https://www.wealthsimple.com/en-ca/learn/how-to-build-credit)

### Route B: Newcomer Credit Card (No Deposit Required)
Several major Canadian financial institutions offer credit card programs designed for newcomers. Eligibility, required documents, credit limits, and other terms vary by institution, so check the bank's current newcomer-card page before applying.

Both routes work for credit-building; the right choice depends on your income documentation and immigration status. Check each bank's current application terms directly.

### Leveraging Existing International Credit (If Applicable)
Nova Credit's Credit Passport® allows newcomers — including permanent residents and foreign workers who have been in Canada less than 5 years — to use their international credit history from select countries to receive higher credit limits on Canadian credit cards. [source](https://www.novacredit.com/corporate-blog/scotiabank-leads-with-first-in-canada-digital-integration-of-nova-credit-for) Scotiabank was the first Canadian bank to partner with Nova Credit and has now embedded this capability directly into its digital credit card application process. [source](https://www.novacredit.com/corporate-blog/scotiabank-leads-with-first-in-canada-digital-integration-of-nova-credit-for) RBC is also collaborating with Nova Credit to leverage Credit Passport® for its Global Credit Connect program. [source](https://www.novacredit.com/canada/business) Country eligibility varies by bank — confirm the list of supported countries directly with the institution.

---

## Step 3 — Use Credit Responsibly Every Month

These behaviours are what actually build your score:

- **Pay in full, on time.** The best way to use a secured credit card is to use it for something you'd buy anyway — like gas or a subscription — then pay it off in full every month. Carrying a balance month to month costs interest and does nothing extra for your credit score. A clean, repeated payment history is exactly what a thin credit file needs. [source](https://nomoredebts.org/blog/learn-about-credit/credit-cards-for-newcomers-to-canada-where-to-start-building-credit)

- **Keep utilization low.** Your credit utilization ratio is the amount of credit you use compared to your total limit. Try to stay well below your limit — RBC's guidance references a 35% credit utilization rule of thumb — and pay off your balance in full each month. [source](https://www.rbcroyalbank.com/en-ca/my-money-matters/life-events/new-to-canada/banking-in-canada/how-to-build-credit-history-as-a-newcomer-to-canada/)

- **Don't open many accounts at once.** You don't need several cards. One credit card used responsibly can be enough to start building a Canadian credit history. [source](https://nomoredebts.org/blog/learn-about-credit/credit-cards-for-newcomers-to-canada-where-to-start-building-credit)

---

## Step 4 — Add More Reporting "Tradelines" Over Time

- **Cell phone plan:** Some postpaid telecom or device-financing accounts may be reported to credit bureaus. Confirm with the provider whether the account is reported before relying on it to build credit.

- **Credit-builder loan:** Some financial institutions offer credit-builder loans. With this loan you don't receive the money upfront — instead, you make regular payments into a savings account. Once the loan term is over, you get access to the money, plus interest. These payments are reported to the credit bureaus and show you can make consistent payments over time. [source](https://welcomeaide.com/en/blog/how-to-build-credit-score-canada-newcomer)

- **Authorized user:** Another option is becoming an authorized user on a trusted person's credit card account. If the primary cardholder's account activity is reported to the credit bureaus under your name, it can contribute to your credit history. [source](https://www.wealthsimple.com/en-ca/learn/how-to-build-credit)

- **Rent reporting (optional):** Services like Borrowell's Rent Advantage can report your monthly rent payments to Equifax, adding another positive data point to your history. [source](https://www.neofinancial.com/blog/how-to-build-your-credit-from-scratch-as-a-canadian-immigrant) Confirm current service availability and any associated fees directly with the provider.

---

## Step 5 — Monitor Your Credit Reports

You can obtain free credit reports from Equifax Canada and TransUnion Canada. FCAC provides the official instructions for ordering a credit report from both bureaus. [source](https://www.canada.ca/en/financial-consumer-agency/services/credit-reports-score/order-credit-report.html)

Checking your own credit report is a soft inquiry and does not affect your credit score. You can request your report from each bureau using the methods listed by FCAC. Contact details: Equifax Canada — 1-800-465-7166; TransUnion Canada — 1-800-663-9980. [source](https://www.canada.ca/en/financial-consumer-agency/services/credit-reports-score/order-credit-report.html)

---

## One Common Pitfall to Avoid

Experts warn newcomers against taking a high-interest loan just to build credit. "The biggest mistake new immigrants can make when trying to build their credit history is accepting a very high interest rate loan. They're much better off getting a secured card, using it and making regular payments. It will be far more effective than having a single loan that could end up costing you thousands in interest." [source](https://www.neofinancial.com/blog/how-to-build-your-credit-from-scratch-as-a-canadian-immigrant)

---

## What to Confirm Before You Decide

| Item | Where to Verify |
|---|---|
| Which newcomer cards you currently qualify for (income, status, length of time in Canada) | Each bank's current newcomer program page (RBC, TD, Scotiabank, CIBC, BMO, etc.) |
| Whether Nova Credit supports your home country | novacredit.com or the participating bank's Nova Credit page |
| Exact secured card deposit minimums, fees, and whether reporting is confirmed | Each card issuer's current product terms |
| Whether a rent-reporting service is available and what it costs | Borrowell or whichever provider you consider, directly |

---

## Confidence

- **Overall confidence:** High
- **Overall confidence reason:** Core steps are well-supported by multiple consistent first-party and reputable sources including FCAC, RBC, Scotiabank, and TD.
- **Section confidence:**
  - *SIN and bank account:* High — consistent across multiple sources
  - *Secured vs. newcomer card routes:* High — supported by bank first-party pages and FCAC-backed guidance
  - *Nova Credit / international credit:* High — sourced from Nova Credit and Scotiabank official press release
  - *Usage habits and utilization:* High — supported by RBC and Credit Counselling Society
  - *Additional tradelines:* Medium — rent reporting and credit-builder loan details are practice-level; exact provider availability and fees should be confirmed directly
  - *Free credit report access:* High — supported by FCAC official guidance and both bureau contacts
